title: Nozick and Wilt Chamberlain
objective: After this level you can explain why Robert Nozick used a basketball star's ticket sales to argue that liberty upsets any fixed pattern of fair shares.
summary: Nozick’s Wilt Chamberlain case argues that free transfers from a just start are just, so liberty upsets patterns such as Rawls’s; Cohen replied that wealth is power.

cards.headline: A million fans each drop a coin in a box. Who could object?
cards.body: Robert Nozick used one basketball star’s ticket sales to challenge every plan for fair shares, including the one you just met in Level 58.

cards.headline: Wilt’s contract
cards.body: In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Nozick asks you to start from whatever distribution you think is just, say, equal shares. Now the star Wilt Chamberlain signs a contract: 25 cents from every ticket goes to him. Over a season, one million fans happily pay. Wilt ends up with $250,000, far more than anyone else.

cards.headline: Where’s the injustice?
cards.body: Is the new distribution unjust? Nozick says no. Everyone started with a just share, each fan paid of their own free will, and anyone who didn’t care to watch kept their money. No one has grounds to complain. That’s his entitlement theory: holdings are just if they were justly acquired or freely transferred, however unequal the result.

cards.headline: Liberty upsets patterns
cards.body: Nozick’s moral: liberty upsets patterns. Any pattern, from equal shares to Rawls’s difference principle, gets broken by people freely spending what they own. Keeping it in place would mean forbidding free exchanges or constantly undoing their results.

cards.headline: Cohen’s reply
cards.body: Critics including G. A. Cohen, in “How Patterns Preserve Liberty” (1977), answered that great wealth is also power. Rich enough, Chamberlain can buy property and pass his fortune to his children, shaping other people’s lives. So free exchanges can end up leaving others less free, and a pattern might protect liberty rather than destroy it.

cards.headline: Nozick and Wilt Chamberlain: the big picture
learned: Fans freely pay Wilt 25 cents each
Just start plus free transfers: just result
Cohen: wealth is power over others

questions.prompt: Match each name with the book or deal linked to it.
questions.explanation: Nozick wrote Anarchy, State, and Utopia, Cohen replied in “How Patterns Preserve Liberty”, and Wilt Chamberlain’s contract gave him 25 cents from every ticket.

questions.prompt: Why does Nozick say Chamberlain’s $250,000 is not unjust?

options.label: Chamberlain works harder than anyone else
Star athletes deserve more than others
Any contract at all is automatically fair
options.rationale: Holdings must be justly acquired or freely transferred.

options.label: Just starting shares plus free payments wrong no one

questions.explanation: Everyone started with a just share and paid voluntarily, so no one has grounds for complaint.

questions.prompt: Nozick says liberty upsets any pattern of shares. Which principle from Level 58 is one such pattern?

options.label: Mill’s harm principle
options.rationale: That limits power over liberty; it isn’t a pattern of shares.

options.label: Han Fei’s rule by impersonal law
options.rationale: That’s about governing, not dividing wealth.

questions.explanation: Rawls’s difference principle fixes a pattern: inequalities must benefit the least advantaged.
